elements.id-string-3: Generation of molecules with desired chemical and biological properties such as high drug-likeness, high binding affinity to target proteins, is critical for drug discovery.
elements.id-string-4: In this paper, we propose a probabilistic generative model to capture the joint distribution of molecules and their properties.
elements.id-string-5: Our model assumes an energy-based model (EBM) in the latent space.
elements.id-string-6: Conditional on the latent vector, the molecule and its properties are modeled by a molecule generation model and a property regression model respectively.
elements.id-string-7: To search for molecules with desired properties,  we propose a sampling with gradual distribution shifting (SGDS) algorithm, so that after learning the model initially on the training data of existing molecules and their properties, the proposed algorithm gradually shifts the model distribution towards the region supported by molecules with desired values of properties.
elements.id-string-8: Our experiments show that our method achieves very strong performances on various molecule design tasks.
elements.id-string-9: The code and checkpoints are available at~\url{https://github.com/deqiankong/SGDS}.
elements.id-string-11: In drug discovery, it is of vital importance to find or design molecules with desired pharmacologic or chemical properties such as high drug-likeness and binding affinity to a target protein.
elements.id-string-12: It is challenging to directly optimize or search over the drug-like molecule space since it is discrete and enormous, with an estimated size on the order of $10^{33}$~\citep{polishchuk2013estimation}.
elements.id-string-13: Recently, a large body of work attempts to tackle this problem.
elements.id-string-14: The first line of work leverages deep generative models to map the discrete molecule space to a continuous latent space, and optimizes molecular properties in the latent space with methods such as Bayesian optimization \citep{gomez2018automatic, kusner2017grammar, jin2018junction}.
elements.id-string-15: The second line of work recruits reinforcement learning algorithms to optimize properties in the molecular graph space directly \citep{you2018graph, de2018molgan, zhou2019optimization, shi2020graphaf, luo2021graphdf}.
elements.id-string-16: A number of other methods have been proposed to optimize molecular properties with genetic algorithms~\citep{nigam2020augmenting}, particle-swarm algorithms~\citep{winter2019efficient}, and specialized MCMC methods \citep{xie2021mars}.
elements.id-string-17: In this work, we propose a method along the first line mentioned above, by learning a probabilistic latent space generative model of molecules and optimizing molecular properties in the latent space.
elements.id-string-18: Given the central role of latent variables in this approach, we emphasize that it is critical to learn a latent space model that captures the data regularities of the molecules.
elements.id-string-19: Thus, instead of assuming a simple Gaussian distribution in the latent space as in prior work~\citep{gomez2018automatic, jin2018junction}, we assume a flexible and expressive energy-based model (EBM)~\citep{lecun2006tutorial,ngiam2011learning,kim2016deep,xie2016theory,kumar2019maximum,nijkamp2019learning,du2019implicit,grathwohl2019your,finn2016connection} in latent space.
elements.id-string-20: This leads to a \textit{latent space energy-based model} (LSEBM) as studied in \cite{pang2020learning,nie2021controllable}, where LSEBM has been shown to model the distributions of natural images and text well.

elements.id-string-34: Going beyond existing latent space energy-based models  \cite{pang2020learning,nie2021controllable}, our work makes two innovations:
elements.id-string-35: First, given our goal of property optimization, we learn a joint distribution of molecules and their properties.
elements.id-string-36: Our model consists of (1) an energy-based model (EBM) in a low-dimensional continuous latent space, (2) a molecule generation model that generates molecule given the latent vector, and (3) a property regression model that predicts the value of the property given the latent vector.
elements.id-string-37: See \cref{fig:SGDS2} for an illustration of the model.
elements.id-string-38: We first learn the initial model on the training data that consist of existing molecules and their properties.
elements.id-string-39: All three components in our model are learned jointly by an approximate maximum likelihood algorithm.
elements.id-string-40: Second, and more importantly, we propose a {\em sampling with gradual distribution shifting} (SGDS) method for molecule design.
elements.id-string-41: We first sample molecules and their property values from the initial model learned on the training data mentioned above.
elements.id-string-42: Then we gradually shift the joint distribution  towards the region supported by molecules with high property values.
elements.id-string-43: Specifically, our method iterates the following steps.
elements.id-string-44: (1) Shift the sampled property values by a small constant towards the desired target value.
elements.id-string-45: (2) Generate molecules given the shifted property values.
elements.id-string-46: (3) Obtain the ground-truth property values of the generated molecules by querying the software.
elements.id-string-47: (4) Update the model parameters by learning from the generated molecules and their ground-truth property values.
elements.id-string-48: Because of the flexibility of the latent space energy-based model, the model can be updated to account for the change of the joint distribution of the generated molecules and their ground-truth property values in the gradual shifting process.
elements.id-string-49: \cref{fig:SGDS4} illustrates the shifting of the distribution of the property values of the generated molecules.
elements.id-string-50: In drug discovery, most often we need to consider multiple properties simultaneously.
elements.id-string-51: Our model can be extended to this setting straightforwardly.
elements.id-string-52: With our method, we only need to add a regression model for each property, while the learning and sampling methods remain the same (see ~\cref{fig:SGDS4}).
elements.id-string-53: We can then simultaneously shift the values of the multiple properties for multi-objective optimization.
elements.id-string-54: We evaluate our method in various settings including single-objective and multi-objective optimization.
elements.id-string-55: Our method outperforms prior methods by significant margins.

elements.id-string-102: As a first step, we need to model or approximate the data distribution of molecules and their properties, $p_{\rm data}(x, y)$.

elements.id-string-104: LSEBM assumes that a latent vector $z \in \sR^d$ in a low dimensional latent space follows an energy-based prior model $p(z)$.
